title: Basic digital citizenship
keyIdea: Being a good digital citizen means staying safe and being kind online. Keep personal information private: your password, address, school and phone number. Behind every screen is a real person with real feelings. If something online feels wrong: stop, block and report, and tell a trusted adult. Think before you post, because posts can stay online.

kid: Some facts about you are private. Your password, your home address, your school and your phone number are private. They could help a stranger find you. Your favourite colour is fine to share.
A real person reads every message. Mean words on a screen hurt just like mean words said out loud. Before you post, ask: would I say this to their face?

Sometimes a message feels wrong. It might be mean, or ask for a photo, or say “Keep it secret.” Stop. Do not reply. Block and report. Then tell a trusted adult, like a parent or a teacher. You will not be in trouble.
People online may not be who they say. Anyone can type any name or age. Only accept friends you know in real life. What you post can stay online, even if you delete it. So think before you post.
adult: This lesson starts digital citizenship: staying safe, kind and responsible online. It matches the IB PYP personal, social and physical education outcome on interactions. In England it covers the primary relationships education topics online relationships and internet safety and harms. The computing curriculum also asks children to use technology safely, respectfully and responsibly.

Key terms for ages 7 to 9: personal (private) information, password, username, trusted adult, cyberbullying, block, report, friend request, stranger and digital footprint. A trusted adult is a grown-up the child knows in real life, such as a parent, carer or teacher.

Common mistakes: thinking some details are harmless, such as a school name or a photo in uniform. Believing a mean comment or a laughing emoji does not hurt because it is only on a screen. Keeping a secret that an online contact asks for, or not telling for fear of losing the tablet. Trusting the name, age or photo on a profile. Thinking deleted posts are gone.

In the lab your child sorts facts into private or OK to share. They pick kind replies and see the real child behind each post. They choose the safe moves when a message asks for a photo. Then they decide on three friend requests and four posts, which build a digital footprint. Every drag or tap has a button twin.

familyTip: Agree a family rule together: if anything online feels wrong, stop, show a grown-up, and nobody is in trouble for telling. Then look at one app your child uses and check who can see their posts.

visual.caption: Private or OK to share? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort private facts, reply kindly to real people, choose safe moves, check friend requests and think before you post.

practice.prompt: Which one should you keep private online?
practice.hint: Which one could help a stranger find you?
practice.explain: Your home address is private, because it tells a stranger where you live. A favourite colour is fine to share.

practice.prompt: You post a photo. {n} friends each share it with {k} other people. How many other people get it?
practice.hint: {n} friends, and each shares with {k} people. Multiply.
practice.explain: {n} friends times {k} people each is {=n*k} people, and you do not know most of them. Posts spread.

practice.prompt: A message says, “Send me a photo. Do not tell your mum.” What should you do?
choices: Do not reply, block, and tell a trusted adult
practice.hint: Think of stop, block and report, tell.
practice.explain: Do not reply, block and report, and tell a trusted adult. A safe person never asks you to keep secrets from your family.

practice.prompt: Kai's password has {a} letters and {b} numbers. How many characters must Kai keep secret?
practice.hint: Add the letters and the numbers.
practice.explain: {a} letters and {b} numbers make {=a+b} characters, and Kai keeps all of them secret.

practice.prompt: Why should you be kind online?
choices: A real person with feelings reads it
Mean words online do not count
practice.explain: A real person with feelings reads every comment, so mean words online hurt just like spoken ones.

pool.prompt: Which one is fine to share in an online game?
pool.hint: Which one does not help anyone find you or get into your account?
pool.explain: Your favourite animal is fine to share. A password and a school name are private.

choices: A parent, carer or teacher you know
Anyone online who says they are a grown-up
A player who gives you free coins
pool.hint: You must know them in real life.
pool.explain: A trusted adult is a parent, carer or teacher you know in real life. Anyone online could be pretending.

pool.prompt: Someone you have never met sends a friend request. Their profile says “Lily, 9”. What should you do?
choices: Say no, and ask a grown-up if unsure
pool.hint: Can you be sure who is really there?
pool.explain: Say no. Anyone can type any name, age or photo, so only accept friends you know in real life.

pool.prompt: Someone keeps posting mean comments about a classmate. What is it called?
pool.explain: It is cyberbullying: being mean to someone again and again online. Do not join in, and tell a trusted adult.

choices: Everything you post and do online
pool.hint: Think of the trail of posts in the lab.
pool.explain: Your digital footprint is everything you post and do online. It can stay there for a long time.

pool.prompt: A mean post is shared by {n} children. Each of them shows {k} more. How many more children see it?
pool.explain: {n} times {k} is {=n*k} more children, so sharing spreads the hurt. Do not share mean posts.

pool.prompt: Mia has {n} online friends. She knows {r} of them in real life. How many are people she has never met?
pool.hint: Take the real-life friends away from all of them.
pool.explain: {n} take away {r} is {=n-r} people Mia has never met. She should ask a grown-up about those.

pool.prompt: You get a message that makes you feel worried. What is the first thing to do?
choices: Forward it to all your friends
pool.explain: Stop and do not reply first. Then block and report, and tell a trusted adult.

pool.prompt: You delete a post. Is it gone for good?
choices: Not always: someone may have saved or shared it
Yes, if it was a photo
pool.hint: Could anyone have copied it first?
pool.explain: Not always. Someone may have saved, screenshotted or shared it before you deleted it, so think before you post.
